# Choosing a roast for espresso

Roast level shapes how an espresso tastes more than almost any other choice a home barista makes. The beans start green and grassy, and heat turns their sugars and acids into the flavours people recognise as coffee. How long the roaster keeps them in the drum decides which of those flavours come forward in the cup.

## Light roasts

Light roasts taste brighter than dark roasts. They keep more of the acidity and the fruit or flower notes of the farm the beans came from, and they often finish clean and short. They are harder to extract, so they usually need a finer grind, a hotter brew water and a slightly longer shot to taste sweet and full.

Many specialty cafes serve light roasts because they show off a single origin. A washed coffee from Ethiopia can taste of lemon and jasmine, and a natural process lot from the same region can taste of strawberry jam. Those notes fade quickly as the roast goes darker.

## Medium roasts

Medium roasts sit in the middle of the range. The acidity softens, caramel and nut flavours appear, and the body gets heavier. They are forgiving to dial in, which makes them a common house espresso for cafes that serve a lot of milk drinks. A medium roast in a flat white tastes of toffee and cocoa.

## Dark roasts

Dark roasts carry roast flavours of their own: chocolate, smoke and sometimes a pleasant bitterness. Much of the origin character is gone by the time oils appear on the surface of the beans. They extract easily, so a coarser grind and a cooler brew water keep the shot from turning harsh and ashy.

Dark roasts also go stale sooner once the bag is open, because the oils on the surface react with air. Buy them in small bags and use them within two weeks of the roast date for the best cup.

## Choosing for your machine

A small home machine with a weak boiler can struggle to keep the water hot enough for a light roast. A machine with stable temperature control handles every roast well. Taste a few shots of each level side by side before you buy a large bag, and write down the grind setting and shot time that worked, so you can repeat it next week.
